A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PASER. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and appendix expansion.

before.justification: V1 reports original recovery experiments, including language modeling, reasoning, mathematics, code generation, quantization, distillation, and component ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds model evaluations, sensitivity studies, component comparisons, and timing measurements.

M1.justification: The clustering, JSD-based budget allocation, efficiency scoring, and concept-consistency filtering remain unchanged, including Algorithm 1. Explicit output-prefix conditioning and newly documented implementation optimizations clarify the retained procedure rather than establish a redesigned method.

E1.justification: Both use Alpaca and LaMini and retain the same language-modeling, seven commonsense-reasoning, mathematics, and code-generation benchmarks. Quantization and distillation recovery already appear in v1. The additional target models and parameter sweeps change experimental configurations, not represented datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: The main selection baselines remain unchanged, but v2 substantially expands evaluated component comparators: Qwen2.5/LLaMA3 embeddings, UMAP/PCA/t-SNE, KLD/Wasserstein distance, and equal/square-root/logarithmic budget allocation (Tables 13, 14, 16, and 17). The earlier clustering-method comparison is retained as Table 15.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluations of LLaMA3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, and Mixtral-8x7B under 25% LLM-Pruner pruning. New protocols include embedding-dimension and temperature sweeps, clustering agreement measured against d=16 using Rand Index, and component timing measurements. Existing recovery budgets, LoRA settings, and evaluation shot counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendices J, K, and L add hyperparameter sensitivity, alternative embedding/reduction/divergence/allocation analyses, and profiling of selection overhead. These test stability, component choices, and computational bottlenecks beyond v1's retained module ablations and clustering comparisons.

E5.justification: Both specify averages over five runs with different seeds and two-tailed independent t-tests using p<0.01 (v1 Appendix K; v2 Appendix P). The new checklist reiterates this practice, and the added sensitivity plots introduce no new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: All twelve original tables retain their numerical results; v1 Tables 11 and 12 become v2 Tables 12 and 15. V2 adds substantial results for newer models, component alternatives, sensitivity, and timing. For example, the new Mixtral comparison reports reasoning scores of 70.87 for PASER and 67.24 for Nuggets; Table 18 reports selection times of 5.83 minutes and 1.18 hours. These are additional results, not improvements to earlier matched scores.

T1.justification: Beyond the retained complexity theorem, v2 Appendix C introduces six formal assumptions, Theorem 2 bounding PASER's loss relative to optimal selection, and a multistep derivation in Equations 8–36. This substantially expands the theoretical substance.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains capability-aware, computationally efficient, consistency-filtered data selection that recovers pruned LLMs using 4%–20% of the original recovery data. The expanded model list and theoretical analysis provide additional support without redefining this central claim.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of MoE recovery, hyperparameter stability, embedding-model cost tradeoffs, diffusion geometry, divergence choices, and budget allocation. Appendix C also interprets its bound as explaining near-optimal recovery. The existing limitations concerning pruning quality, scalability, recovery bias, and concept-consistency failures are retained.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies d=16, temperature 1.0, typical cluster counts, concept-extraction limits, and a 0.75 similarity threshold. It documents large-dataset optimizations, selection-stage runtimes, and GPU memory requirements, while replacing the named RTX GPU description with memory-based hardware reporting. The code-access pointer changes from GitHub to an anonymous repository; availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: V2 adds references on knowledge localization, Mixtral, Qwen2.5, and Wasserstein distance, and sharpens the explanation of why generic instruction quality may not target pruning damage. The related-work organization and overall positioning against generic instruction selection remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized abstract, introduction, and methodology edits and renames negative transfer mitigation to negative tuning effects mitigation. It adds a contents list and checklist and nests the earlier clustering comparison within a broader component-selection appendix. Main section order and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensive resizing and relocation of tables and figures. Figure 1 is revised, and six new tables plus Figures 5 and 6 are added. Figures 2–4 retain identical graphical content despite their changed placement and size.

improvement.justification: The added controlled comparisons, sensitivity studies, selection profiling, and implementation settings improve empirical assessment and reproducibility. However, Appendix C drops the cross-cluster error term between Equations 35–36 although Assumption 2 only bounds it. Appendix L also calls 68.1%/92.6% savings overall savings while excluding selection overhead; Table 18 implies approximately 61.1%/90.6% when included. These weaknesses temper the practical gains to a limited net improvement.
